set.plain: At one big Colorado hospital, 2,567 emergency visits over five years were judged to be at least partly due to cannabis. Only 238 of them, about 1 in 11, were linked to eating or drinking cannabis; the rest were linked to smoking or vaping it. Compared with the smoking and vaping visits, the edible visits more often involved being very intoxicated, sudden mental-health symptoms such as acute anxiety or psychosis, or heart symptoms, and less often involved vomiting or being admitted to hospital. But because far more visits involved smoking or vaping, most visits for each of those problems still involved smoking or vaping. Two papers describe a slower start and a longer-lasting effect from eating cannabis than from inhaling it, and some case reports describe people eating more after feeling nothing at first, but no study here timed effects in patients or counted how often people eat more. A laboratory test of 75 edibles bought in three US cities in 2014 found that only about 1 in 6 held the amount of THC printed on the label: about 1 in 4 held more, and about 3 in 5 held less, some almost none. Calls to US poison centres about children under 6 who ate cannabis edibles rose every year, from about 200 in 2017 to about 3,000 in 2021. Most of the children were 1 to 4 years old and ate the edible at home; more than 1 in 5 were admitted to hospital, 35 needed a breathing tube, and no deaths were reported. These are only the calls that were made, and the study could not tell how much of the rise came from changes in the law, the pandemic or more people calling. The hospital study and the overview could not count how many people took each form, how much they took, what was in the product, or who never went to hospital, so they cannot say how likely any form is to lead to a hospital visit, and they did not compare either form with people who do not use cannabis.

statement
For children, the overview gives only second-hand figures (poison-centre calls, and one children's hospital, rising over 2005 to 2015) and says emergency visits for children remain relatively low.

A laboratory test of products, read with its July 2015 correction (whose wording is followed where the saved letter differs), measured 75 labelled edible products of 47 brands (baked goods, drinks, candy or chocolate) bought in August to October 2014 at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, in markets the authors call unregulated. Against the THC printed on the package, 13 (17%) were within 10%, 17 (23%) held more than the label said (on average 28% more, at most 55% more) and 45 (60%) held less (on average about half the labelled amount: 47% less in the table's overall row, about 53% less from its city rows, editors' arithmetic; at most 99% less, some with almost none). Products holding more than their label were commonest in Los Angeles (9 of 20) and products holding less in Seattle (18 of 23, where 1 product was within 10%); San Francisco had 8 of 32 within 10% (χ² = 12.94, P = .01). Only 13 products printed a CBD content, and none held it within 10% (4 more, 9 less; editors' arithmetic), although 44 of the 75 contained some CBD. Whole packages were mixed before testing, so the test cannot say how evenly THC was spread between pieces or servings (two samples of the same mixed package differed by more than 10% in 37 products, which were then analysed whole), and it measured no effects in people: the authors' statements that products with less THC may not give the intended medical benefit and that products with more put patients at risk of adverse effects are their inference. The sample was not random and may not generalize, as the authors say, and the cost of the testing was covered by Werc Shop Laboratories, with which four of the six authors are affiliated (see funding). Children: calls to the 55 US poison centres about children younger than 6 who ate cannabis edibles rose every year, from 207 in 2017 to 590, 983, 2,209 and 3,054 in 2021 (7,043 in all), and from 0.2 to 3.6 in every 1,000 calls about children of that age, while those calls overall fell (956,871 in 2017, 846,296 in 2021). The children's median age was 3 years (2-year-olds were the largest group, 27.7%; under 1 year, 1.9%), about half were girls, and 90.7% had eaten the product in their own home (97.1% in a home, their own or another). In the poison centres' grading, 2.2% of all 7,043 had a major effect and 21.9% a moderate one (together 35.1% of the 4,827 followed to a known outcome, editors' arithmetic); 22.7% were admitted to hospital (8.1% to critical care), 35 children were intubated, and no deaths were reported. Among those followed up, reduced alertness (CNS depression) was recorded in 70.0%, a fast heart rate in 11.4%, vomiting in 9.5%, slowed breathing in 3.1% and seizures in 1.6%. These are reported calls only, which the authors call an underestimate, and 30.4% were not followed to a known outcome. The authors could not count cases by state; they write that the rise is believed to be associated with more states allowing adult recreational use, that quarantines and school or daycare closures during the pandemic may have played a part, and that it is unknown whether more reporting or less stigma contributed; their data cannot separate these. The shares graded moderate (15.9% against 23.8%) or major (1.6% against 2.4%), and the shares admitted, were higher in 2020 to 2021 than in 2017 to 2019; for the change in where children were treated the authors write that it is unknown why it occurred, suggesting among other things more THC per package or more products bought, more severe effects, or clinicians' comfort and bed availability, and a comparison of later with earlier years of a rising series cannot single out the pandemic. Which products were eaten, how much THC they held and where they came from were not reported. The overview's earlier, second-hand child figures (2005 to 2015) pointed the same way.

evidence_add.extracted: Products, not people: dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle were picked at random from an Internet directory until three per city were found that sold at least one edible in each of three categories (baked goods, beverages, candy or chocolate) with a specific delta-9-THC content on the label. Between August and October 2014, purchasers with a physician's letter and no history of buying edibles bought as wide a variety as possible within $400 per city; purchasers, but not dispensary staff, knew the products would be tested. Whole packages were homogenized and two samples tested by high-performance liquid chromatography, averaged and scaled to the product's weight; where the two differed by more than 10% (37 products) the whole product was analysed. Within 10% of the label counted as accurate, more than 10% above as underlabelled and more than 10% below as overlabelled.
